about.heading: About me
about.intro: I studied psychology and then taught myself to program. Both turned out to be about the same thing: building models of something complicated that are simple enough to reason about, and finding out where they break.
about.learning: I started with C++, moved to C# and SQL Server, and from there to ASP.NET Core and the layered architecture I still work in. No bootcamp and no degree in it — a long sequence of projects, each one larger than the last, and a habit of reading other people's code.
about.psychology: The degree shows up in design decisions more than in code. In the AI workspace, every answer the assistant gives carries the document and the page it came from, because an answer nobody can check is an answer nobody acts on. Confidence without a source is a liability, not a feature — and that is a claim about people, not about software.
about.looking: Freelance projects, remote roles, or local work. I live in Aksaray and I am open to positions in Ankara.

projects.heading: Projects
projects.intro: Two systems, both built end to end. One is a distributed AI workspace; the other is a desktop application over SQL Server. Together they are most of what I do.

aiWorkspace.name: AI Autonomous Workspace
aiWorkspace.problem: Documents accumulate faster than anyone reads them. This workspace stores them, indexes what is in them, and answers questions about them with the source attached.
aiWorkspace.architecture: ASP.NET Core in four layers — Domain, Application, Infrastructure and Api — with a Python FastAPI service for the retrieval work, PostgreSQL and Qdrant in Docker, and the language model running locally. No third-party AI provider: the whole pipeline runs on its own hardware.
aiWorkspace.scale: 598 files · 189 C# · 80 Python · 85 test files · 74 merged pull requests
aiWorkspace.result: Measured on a running stack rather than estimated: a 35-page PDF goes from upload to searchable in 32.6 seconds, and every answer comes back with the page it was drawn from.
aiWorkspace.scope: Feature-complete through its ninth sprint. The tenth is release preparation, so the system is built and verified but not yet deployed.

restaurant.name: Restaurant Management
restaurant.problem: Purchasing and inventory for a restaurant, as a Windows desktop application the staff could use in their own language.
restaurant.architecture: Three tiers — forms, business logic, data access — with every database call going through a stored procedure and none through inline SQL.
restaurant.scale: 9 forms · 10 tables · 37 stored procedures · RDLC reports
restaurant.notable: The interface is Arabic and right-to-left throughout, which is where I first learned how much of a layout is direction-dependent.
